statedGuarantee: SEAgent claims to prevent privilege escalation in LLM-based agent systems, defined as any agent invocation action outside the oracle-minimal set required to fulfill the user's intent. It maintains a per-round directed information-flow graph (the System View) over users, agents, tools and RAG databases; statically labels tools (Object/Action/Sensitivity/Privacy/Integrity), agents (Integrity) and RAG databases (Integrity/Privacy); and runs a Decision Engine that matches SELinux-style path-plus-Boolean-rule policies against that graph before each tool invocation or inter-agent message, emitting allow, ask, or deny. It reports 0% attack success rate on InjecAgent and AgentDojo against indirect prompt injection and RAG poisoning, and a case-study block of a confused-deputy attack in a multi-agent system.
advertisedRhetoric: "a mandatory access control (MAC) framework built upon attribute-based access control (ABAC)" and "SEAgent employs a policy-driven Mandatory Access Control (MAC) mechanism to enforce fine-grained rules over the execution flow graph of the agent system." The OS framing is sustained throughout: policy syntax is "inspired by SELinux ( Smalley et al., 2001 )", the Action attribute uses "terminology aligned with Linux file permissions", the labels are "inspired by the classic information security models like Bell-LaPadula ( , 2025 ) and Biba ( , 2025 )", and Figure 1 introduces the problem via Linux/Unix kernel privilege escalation and Android confused-deputy IPC. Enforcement is characterized as "deterministic and auditable policy enforcement, which is particularly valuable for high-assurance and safety-critical applications".
tierSpan: When a new tool invocation is detected in the agent system, the Decision Engine analyzes the structure of the System View and compares it with security policies stored in the Policy DB .
cheapestDefeat: GUARANTEE: no agent invocation action outside the user-intent-minimal set is executed. MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the Decision Engine's pre-invocation check against the System View graph. The graph is built exclusively from actions the agent framework itself emits -- 'a new node instance corresponding to this invocation (uniquely identified, e.g., by a UUID) is added to the graph, along with an edge from the calling agent' -- so it models declared tool calls and inter-agent messages and nothing else. CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: do not attempt to defeat the engine at all; obtain one permitted invocation of a tool whose downstream effects the graph cannot see. The paper's own InjecAgent label table registers a TerminalExecute tool (LOCAL / EXECUTE / HIGH / UNFILTERED). Once that call is allowed -- by matching no policy at all ('If no policies are matched after checking the entire database, the engine defaults to allowing the action.'), or by a user clicking 'Allow once : The action is allowed for this round only.' -- every file write, further process spawn, and network connection made by the resulting child process occurs with no node, no edge, and no policy evaluation. No signature is forged and no label is tampered with. Two cheaper-still variants: (a) Assumption 1, 'Tools are provided by a trusted SDK.', means a tool whose real behavior exceeds its static label is simply outside the model; (b) labels 'cannot be updated dynamically at runtime', so a tool that becomes dangerous mid-round retains its benign label. TIER OF THE DEFEATED MECHANISM: an in-framework chokepoint on the agent's tool-dispatch path. Nothing in the design sits below the process -- there is no kernel module, no LSM hook, no syscall interposition, no seccomp or namespace confinement, and no label store the OS consults. The term 'mandatory access control' here denotes only that the policy is not modifiable by the agent; it does not denote kernel enforcement. Any effect reachable without traversing the dispatcher is unbound. Score T3.
placementSpan: poison the external environment to manipulate tool returns

coverageSpans.E1: LOCAL: The tool operates on local system resources (e.g., file I/O). -- and WRITE: Modify system state or content (e.g., updating configurations, deleting files). Declared file-writing tools are labeled and pass the chokepoint, but writes performed inside a tool's own implementation or by a process it spawns add no node to the System View, and unmatched flows are allowed by default.
coverageSpans.E2: EXECUTE: Perform a function that triggers observable behavior (e.g., sending messages or executing transactions). The benchmark tool table includes TerminalExecute (LOCAL / EXECUTE / HIGH / UNFILTERED), so the top-level spawn is a mediated invocation. Descendant spawns are categorically invisible: the System View gains nodes only from agent-emitted tool calls and inter-agent messages, so the depth rule caps this at partial.
coverageSpans.E3: EXTERNAL: The tool interacts with external APIs or web services. Egress through declared tools is mediated, and the Email Data Stealing Protection Policy specifically "blocks flows in which an agent reads sensitive personal data and attempts to exfiltrate it via the email sending tool." Egress by a descendant process, or by a tool's own internals, traverses no chokepoint. Depth rule caps at partial.
coverageSpans.E4: Users can customize or expand these rules to fit their operational needs -- the paper never names version control anywhere, and no git tool appears in any of the four benchmark label appendices. Scored partial only on the charitable reading that the mechanism is defined over an arbitrary toolset, so a registered VCS-push tool would be labeled EXTERNAL/EXECUTE and mediated like any other declared call; a push issued by a shell subprocess would still be unmediated. A strict coder should score this not-covered. See notes.
coverageSpans.E5: the setting agent attempts to invoke the Uninstall_App tool -- install/uninstall appears as an ordinary labeled tool, so the top-level invocation is mediated. Third-party install is discussed only for agents from the AIOS Agent Hub, and only at labeling time, not runtime. Post-install hooks and their network activity are descendant processes and are never modeled, so the E5 depth rule caps this at partial.
coverageSpans.E6: PERSONAL: Sensitive personal information (e.g., health records, schedules, passwords) -- credentials are recognized as a Privacy value on tool output, the benchmark toolset includes password tools (NortonIdentitySafeSharePassword, NortonIdentitySafeSearchPasswords), and the email-exfiltration policy blocks a read-personal-then-send flow. But no credential list is published: environment variables, config files, keychains and cloud metadata endpoints are never enumerated, and credentials read inside a tool or by a subprocess produce no graph node. The undefined-list rule caps at partial.
coverageSpans.E7: This policy prohibits untrusted agents from invoking any tool with sensitivity above LOW. The use of wildcards in the path pattern ensures that indirect privilege escalation paths, such as confused deputy scenarios, are also covered. This is the paper's strongest cell -- inter-agent messages are first-class actions in the formal model and edges in the System View, agents carry an Integrity label, and a confused-deputy block is demonstrated. It is still partial: the model contains no spawn action (a new agent node appears only when messaged), so creating a sub-agent is not itself an intercepted event, an agent instantiated inside a tool's implementation or by a subprocess is invisible, and the default-allow fallthrough applies here as everywhere.

schneider.surrogate: A per-invocation, prefix-decidable safety property over the observed trace: no tool invocation or inter-agent message is executed whose path in the current-round System View graph matches a deny policy whose Boolean attribute rule evaluates true. This is exactly what the Decision Engine monitors and it is genuinely monitor-enforceable -- it is decided on each action from the finite graph accumulated so far, with a defined default ("If no policies are matched after checking the entire database, the engine defaults to allowing the action.").
schneider.objective: Two advertised objectives sit outside the enforceable class. (1) The headline definition of least privilege relative to intent: an action counts as escalation if it is not in T_q, and the paper concedes T_q "is oracle-defined and often not known in advance, making defense against such attacks challenging" -- a monitor cannot decide membership in an unobservable oracle set, so this is not a safety property over the trace. (2) An explicit information-flow hyperproperty: "SEAgent enforces user-level non-interference via user-level isolation". Non-interference is the canonical non-monitorable hyperproperty (it quantifies over pairs of executions), and notably this is the one attack vector the authors do not test -- they "omit further experiments for this vector". The Bell-LaPadula/Biba-inspired Privacy and Integrity labels advertise confidentiality and integrity flow control of the same non-monitorable kind.

notes:
FULL TEXT: retrieved and coded from the complete arXiv HTML v1 (arXiv:2601.11893v1 [cs.CR] 17 Jan 2026), 907KB of source, all sections plus Appendices A-K including the four benchmark tool-label tables. Not coded from the abstract. Authors: Zimo Ji, Daoyuan Wu, Wenyuan Jiang, Pingchuan Ma, Zongjie Li, Yudong Gao, Shuai Wang, Yingjiu Li (HKUST / Lingnan / ETH Zurich / ZJUT / U. Oregon).

WHY THIS IS THE HEADLINE DEMOTION ROW -- CONFIRMED, AND MORE PRECISELY THAN THE BRIEF ANTICIPATED. The brief predicted 'mandatory access control with no kernel, no label store, no reference monitor below the process.' The text bears this out exactly. The OS vocabulary is not incidental: policy syntax is inspired by SELinux, the Action values READ/WRITE/EXECUTE are explicitly 'aligned with Linux file permissions', the labels invoke Bell-LaPadula and Biba, and the paper's own Figure 1 motivates the work with Linux kernel privilege escalation and Android IPC confused deputy. Yet every one of those borrowed mechanisms was kernel-resident in its original, and none is here. The label store is a static table consulted by a Python-level Decision Engine; the reference monitor is the agent framework's tool dispatcher; there is no LSM hook, no syscall interposition, no namespace, no seccomp filter, no container. T2 to T3 is a two-level demotion from the advertised strength and it is the cleanest instance of borrowed-kernel-vocabulary in the corpus so far.

THE SHARPEST SINGLE ARTIFACT for the demotion row: the paper's own Appendix I registers a TerminalExecute tool labeled LOCAL / EXECUTE / HIGH / UNFILTERED. A framework calling itself mandatory access control that mediates the invocation of a terminal but not the process the terminal creates has drawn its boundary above, not below, the thing MAC exists to bound. This is a single-quote demonstration that the enforcement unit is the declared call, not the capability.

WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN, for the adjudicator:

1. E4 (VCS push) is my weakest cell and the one most likely to be flipped. The paper never mentions version control; no git tool appears in any benchmark appendix. The coding rule says a system that simply does not address an effector scores not-covered. I scored partial because the mechanism is genuinely generic over the toolset (the formal model defines the tool set as arbitrary, and the authors write that they 'do not take credits for their exhaustiveness' and that users 'can customize or expand these rules'), so a registered git-push tool would be labeled and mediated like any other. That is a defensible charitable reading, not an invented one -- but a strict coder should score E4 not-covered and I would not argue hard. Flagging explicitly rather than burying it.

2. E5 is partial on the same generic-mechanism reasoning plus the concrete Uninstall_App tool in Figure 4's worked example. Package install hooks specifically are never discussed.

3. All seven effectors landing on partial is a real result, not coder laziness. It follows from one structural fact: SEAgent mediates exactly one thing -- the framework's own dispatch of declared agent actions -- and mediates it uniformly. So every effector with a declared tool gets the same treatment (mediated at the call, unmediated below it), and none reaches covered because the depth rule and the covert-channel rule both bite in the same place for all of them. A reviewer who sees seven partials should read that as a uniform ceiling, not a hedge.

4. E7 deserves credit where due. The MAS handling is the paper's genuine contribution and its strongest cell: inter-agent messages are first-class in the formal model, the wildcard path patterns really do catch transitive confused-deputy chains, and prior work (IsolateGPT, CaMeL, SecAlign) is shown failing where SEAgent holds. I kept it at partial because the model has no spawn action -- an agent node enters the graph only on being messaged -- and because default-allow applies. But if any cell in this coding is arguably harsh, it is this one.

TIER, WORKED EXPLICITLY (per the brief's requirement): guarantee = no invocation outside the intent-minimal set executes. Mechanism that must fail = the pre-invocation Decision Engine check over the System View. Cheapest adversary action = not defeating that check but routing the effect around it, e.g. via a permitted EXECUTE tool whose child process the graph never models, reached through the documented default-allow or a single user 'Allow once'. Tier of the mechanism that action defeats = an in-process application chokepoint on the dispatch path. T3.

HONESTY CREDITS TO THE AUTHORS, which do not change the score. They state the static-label limitation plainly ('cannot be updated dynamically at runtime'), concede T_q is oracle-defined and unavailable in advance, decline to claim policy exhaustiveness, document the default-allow fallthrough rather than hiding it, disclose both false positives by name (the Wikipedia tool mislabeled UNFILTERED), and release an artifact. Under the covert-channel rule, documented honesty about an excluded channel still yields partial rather than covered -- the exclusion is honest and the gap is still open.

EVIDENCE GRADE L2: behavioral confirmation on four benchmarks (InjecAgent 80 tools, AgentDojo 74 tools, API-Bank 52 tools/214 tasks, AWS multi-agent), reporting 0% ASR, FP rates, token and latency overhead, plus a released artifact that would support L1 source inspection. No reproducible bypass of SEAgent itself is demonstrated. Note the paper does demonstrate L3-grade reproducible bypasses -- but against the BASELINES (SecAlign via direct injection, IsolateGPT via Hub-level and anonymous-Spoke RAG poisoning, CaMeL via argument manipulation of a correctly planned call), not against its own system. That asymmetry is worth carrying into the SoK: SEAgent's central empirical contribution is a set of working bypasses of three named prior defenses.

PLACEMENT: primary A2 because that is what the evaluation actually tests at scale -- indirect prompt injection through tool returns and RAG poisoning, across InjecAgent and AgentDojo. Secondary A3 (untrusted third-party agent carrying a malicious system prompt: modeled, policy-covered, and demonstrated, but by case study only, since the authors note the lack of large-scale MAS benchmarks). Secondary A1 (malicious user issuing direct prompt injection: claimed handled by user-level isolation, but the authors 'omit further experiments for this vector'). A4 and A5 are explicitly outside the threat model -- the adversary is assumed 'without the ability to directly interfere with the runtime execution'.
